topic: Four-day work week trials: reported effects on productivity, revenue, employee wellbeing and retention, and limits of the evidence

key_points.point: The 2022 UK pilot covered 61 companies and about 2,900 employees for six months on a 100-80-100 model (full pay, 80% of hours, maintained output).
In the UK pilot revenue was roughly flat (average +1.4% for the 23 firms reporting) and staff turnover fell 57% with sick days down 65%.
In the UK pilot 71% of employees reported less burnout, and 56 of 61 organisations were still on a four-day week a year later.

A 2025 Nature Human Behaviour study (141 organisations, 2,896 employees, six countries) found lower burnout and better job satisfaction, mental and physical health versus 12 control firms, persisting at 12 months.
The study attributes wellbeing gains to better sleep, less fatigue and higher self-assessed work ability, with larger hour cuts linked to larger gains; trial staff cut about five hours a week.

Iceland's 2015-2019 trials (about 2,500 workers) reported unchanged or improved output and better wellbeing, per think tank Autonomy, which says 86% of workers now have shorter hours or the right to them.

Germany's 2024 pilot (45 organisations, six months, Münster evaluation) found perceived productivity stable or up and better life satisfaction, but revenue and sick-day changes were not statistically significant.

Productivity evidence is thin: the Nature study did not analyse company-level productivity, and UK and German productivity claims rest largely on self-report, revenue from a subset, or managers' perceptions.

Participants self-selected into trials and were mostly small, office-based or professional-services firms in English-speaking countries, so results may overstate effects and may not generalise to retail, healthcare or manufacturing.

Trials were short (six months, one 12-month follow-up), mostly lacked randomised controls, and were organised by advocacy groups; the Nature study's authors call for randomised or government-sponsored trials.

Proponents reply that some pilots (Portugal, Germany) had controls and that a single productivity metric is infeasible across industries, so they use revenue, sickness data, managerial interviews and organisational indicators.
Critics note the model is hard to apply where cover is needed, such as emergency services, transport, logistics and healthcare, where costs may rise.
